value.loc: Sec. 6.1 Synthetic Data, p. 2763; Sec. 4, p. 2760
value.quote: Voters approve (resp. rank) candidates based on their estimations.
value.note: The noisy observation model gives voters positions p(v) and estimates p_v(c) with notation separate from the approval set, and Sec. 4 says a missing approval may be an error ('i does not know who c is'). Elsewhere ballots are called 'approval preferences' and taken as given.

C2.4.reason: The paper uses separate notation for voters' positions/estimates and their approval sets (Sec. 6.1) and says ballots may contain errors (Sec. 4), which meets DIST.

value.quote_behav: Voters approve (resp. rank) candidates based on their estimations.
value.note: Voters only submit approval ballots, taken as given in the axiomatic part and generated by a fixed rule (approve iff estimated distance at most r) in the synthetic model; this fixed behaviour is said in words.

C6.VOT.reason: Voter behaviour is fixed, and the rule by which voters form their ballots is stated in words in Sec. 6.1, so behav_stated is EXPLICIT rather than IMPLICIT.

value.quote: each voter approves adjacent candidates, an analogue of singlepeakedness
value.note: The claims that the rules find an ideological axis (for polls, parliament, the Supreme Court) need that approvals reflect proximity on an ideological axis; the paper states this in the abstract, formalises it in the noisy observation model (Sec. 6.1) and states it for justices in Sec. 6.3. Claims about which rule is better follow from the axiomatic results; no assumption on strategy, information or utilities is needed.

C9.2.reason: The one needed assumption, that approval ballots reflect ideological proximity so the best-fitting axis is an ideological ordering, is stated in the abstract and formalised in Sec. 6.1, so no needed assumption is unstated.
